senses: To incorrectly or badly hit.
ety: From mis- + hit.
examples: Although Collins mishit the ball, he still managed to pocket the red.

senses: Characteristic of a husband; proper and fitting for a husband; marital.
ety: From Middle English housbondly, equivalent to husband + -ly.
examples: One thing she still would not allow was that horrible erotic act which was a commonplace of American and European films, but she took complaisantly enough now to his other husbandly advances.

He strives for husbandly allure in slow-motion ballads: “Love You Gently” and the role-reversing “Trading Places,” in which he calls for her to be the aggressive one and offers to make breakfast the next morning.
As a result, analogies between royal, paternal, and husbandly authority were frequently drawn.

senses: Reminiscent of the punk subculture; slightly punk.
ety: From punk + -ish.
examples: It certainly had merit as a punkish shouter with its machine-gun-spatter underbeat.

senses: Of wind: blowing in gusts; blustery; tempestuous.
Characterized by or occurring in instances of sudden strong expression.
Bombastic, verbose.
ety: From gust + -y.
examples: A change evidently came over the countess's thoughts; her thin lips grew white (her eyes remained the same), and her voice when she spoke evidently surprised even herself by the violence of its gusty outburst.
The spirit becomes an ingrained part of one's life, not subject to gusty moods and feelings, but a habitual part of life.
From the vigorous, warm, gusty oratory of the Gallican apologists, we pass into a thinner and cooler and quieter atmosphere, that of the Spanish lecture-room.

senses: A herbaceous plant, Rubia tinctorum, native to Asia, cultivated for a red-purple dye (alizarin) obtained from the root.
The root of the plant, used as a medicine or a dye.
A dye made from the plant.
A deep reddish colour, like that of the dye.
ety: From Middle English mader, madere, mædere, from Old English mædere, mæddre, mædre, from Proto-Germanic *madarǭ (compare Swedish måra, Old Norse / Icelandic maðra), from Proto-Indo-European *modʰro-, cognate with Proto-Slavic *modrъ (“blue”), and compare Irish madar (“madder”), Latvian madara (“madder”).
examples: Their armour was stained with madder, in such wise that they seemed bathed in blood.
Her big head has coloured to a dim and dreadful madder.

senses: A Vedic poet and seer who composed Rigvedic hymns, who alone or with others invokes the deities with poetry of a sacred character.
ety: From Sanskrit ऋषि (ṛ́ṣi), from Proto-Indo-Iranian *r̥šíš (whence Avestan 𐬆𐬭𐬆𐬴𐬌𐬴 (ərəṣ̌iṣ̌, “seer”)), probably related to अर्षति (árṣati, “to flow, pour”).
examples: The rishi asked one unfathomable question after another, until both he and his audience were reduced to the silence of unknowing.

senses: Tall and thin, especially so as to cause physical awkwardness.
ety: An American English alteration of gangling.
examples: A rangy, gangly, Scandinavian youth of a sailor, droop-shouldered, six feet six and slender as a lath, with pallid eyes of palest blue and skin and hair attuned to the same colour scheme, joined Kwaque in his work.
He was a tall, gangly, shy satirist who mumbled to you with his head turned away and always said funny things.
She was gangly and wild and walked with her wrists turned inside out...

senses: Frozen fruit juice, sometimes mixed with egg whites, eaten as dessert or between courses of a meal.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French sorbet, borrowed from Italian sorbetto, borrowed from Ottoman Turkish شربت (şerbet), borrowed from Classical Persian شَرْبَت (šarbat), borrowed from Arabic شَرْبَة (šarba), from شَرِبَ (šariba). Doublet of sherbet and sharbat, related to syrup.
examples: After dinner we had an orange sorbet that was very refreshing.

senses: The act or process of dehumanizing.
ety: From de- + humanization or dehumanize + -ation or de- + human + -ization.
examples: The essence of dehumanization is not to see someone, to render him inconsequential and invisible.

senses: A polyester film.
ety: From a trademark.
examples: In the far infrared a self-supporting layer, such as a sheet of mylar stretched over a plane circular surface, is widely used.

senses: An object meant to be carried by a single person.
ety: From man + pack.
examples: We decide to stop in Chemainus for lunch, so we tie up at the public wharf, set security, grab the manpacks, and stroll into the pretty little town... enjoying the stretch.
The operating voltage for the manpack radio is 13.5 volts from the primary battery.

senses: To run with a light pattering noise; to skitter.
ety: Alteration of scuttle.
examples: We saw a rat scuttering into a dark corner as we turned on the lights.
I scuttered all the way to Dallory, and scuttered back again ; and I don’t think I stopped to speak to a single soul, but Timothy Wilks.”
When the birds, especially the starlings, ate them in vast quantities, the results were often spectacular — they scuttered everywhere and over everything.

senses: A structure consisting of two stone pillars supporting a horizontal stone.
ety: From Ancient Greek τρίλιθος (trílithos, “of three stones”). Compare the Baalbek trilithon.
examples: Within the sarsen circle are the five impressive trilithons, forming a horseshoe-shaped ring of huge stones.

senses: Synonym of diplomat.
A person trained in diplomatics.
ety: Borrowed from French diplomatiste, or from diplomat(ic) + -ist.
examples: She flung back the fortnight on his hands as if he had been an idler indifferent to dates, instead of an active young diplomatist who, to respond to her call, had had to hew his way through a very jungle of engagements!
Diplomatists have no right to complain of mere lies; it is their own fault, if, educated as they are, the lies deceive them; but they complain bitterly of traps.

senses: A line at the head of a newspaper or magazine article carrying the writer's name.
ety: From by- + line.
examples: Paste Magazine opted not to put a byline on its harsh review of Swift’s album, citing safety concerns for the writer.

senses: A pin or fastener for the hair.
A very tight bend in a road; a hairpin bend.
An elongated horizontal v-shaped sign placed underneath a staff to indicate a crescendo or decrescendo.
ety: From hair + pin, 1788 (as hair pin). Adjective sense 1906 in hairpin turn etc.
examples: The variety of angles in the course, from slow bends to hairpins, will both test your skill as a driver and allow you the opportunity to pass other carts.

senses: To make accustomed; to accustom; to familiarize.
ety: From Middle English habituat(e) (“physically established or present”) (borrowed from Late Latin habituātus, perfect passive participle of habituō (“to bring into a condition or habit of body”)). See -ate (verb-forming suffix).
examples: My first quarter at Lowood seemed an age; and not the golden age either; it comprised an irksome struggle with difficulties in habituating myself to new rules and unwonted tasks.

senses: A hunter or hunter's attendant.
A sharpshooter, a rifleman, light infantry.
ety: A borrowing from German Jäger (“hunter”). Related to English yacht. Compare yager, yagger.
examples: These were the mounted Hessian riflemen, the dreaded Jaegers.
St. Louis, however, was not a place where such things could be kept secret for long. By early March, Democratic papers carried reports of a terrifying new battalion known as the Black Jaegers --

senses: Spry, nimble.
ety: From slip + -y. Compare Old English slipiġ (“slippy, slimy, viscid”).
examples: Well, come on then, let's look slippy.

senses: The act of feminizing, or the state of being feminized.
The increasing in female population or participation.
ety: From feminize + -ation.
examples: America is rapidly becoming the manosphere, but sure, let’s go after the “feminization” of culture.

senses: An assumption made beforehand; a preliminary conjecture or speculation.
The act of presupposing.
ety: From Middle French présupposition, from Latin praesuppositio, from the past participle stem of praesuppōnere (“to presuppose”).
examples: He made one cardinal error in his presuppositions about the relation between language and perception, but in this he was far from alone.

senses: A structure which serves as a cover or lid.
ety: Borrowed from Latin operculum.
examples: I lifted the circular operculum from its place and laid it carefully on the bale.

senses: An ancient site used for burying the dead, particularly if consisting of elaborate grave monuments.
ety: Borrowed from Koine Greek νεκρόπολις (nekrópolis, “city of the dead, cemetery”) (used to describe part of the city of Alexandria, Egypt), from Ancient Greek νεκρός (nekrós, “dead”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *neḱ- (“to disappear; to perish”)) + πόλις (pólis, “city”) (ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *tpelH- (“city; fortification”)). The English word is analysable as necro- + -polis, and is cognate with French nécropole, German Nekropolis, Late Latin necropolis. The plural form necropoleis is derived from Ancient Greek νεκροπόλεις (nekropóleis).
examples: What would be the result if one attempted to determine the physical character of that people from a study of the remains in their necropoli?
The great cemeteries or necropolises (literally, "cities of the dead") adjacent to the major Etruscan cities such as Cerveteri and Tarquinia are the most visible relics of this civilization.
Separate fractions of dentine and enamel of 12 individuals from the necropolis of Sion (Valais, Switzerland) have been analyzed for Pb and Sr isotope compositions.

senses: A dish, commonly associated with French cuisine, consisting of edible snails.
A snail (often Helix pomatia) used in preparation of that dish.
ety: Borrowed from French escargot.
examples: J. is dating P. at NYU and modeling on the side. They're planning to meet us in Paris for spring break so J. can go to some look-sees (and eat some escargot, obv.).

senses: A book of public records.
ety: Learned borrowing from Latin liber (“the inner bark of a tree; book”). See libel.
examples: The libers of wills above mentioned are estimated to contain 600 pages, which would make the average cost, per liber, $636.

senses: A roll or twist of hair worn at the nape of the neck; a bun.
ety: Borrowed from French chignon circa 1780, when the hairstyle was in fashion.
examples: The chignon cannot be confounded with other artificialities which ladies put on and off.
Madame du Barry could not merely be credited with inventing the chignons which bear her name.
If I close my eyes I can see Marie today as I saw her then. Round, rosy face, snub nose, dark hair piled up in a chignon.

senses: A person who can transform into an animal.
ety: Coined by J. K. Rowling for her Harry Potter series as a blend of animal + magus. Term is introduced in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban (1999).
examples: You know it better as Harry Potter. / It’s full of werewolves, and animaguses, / And men with two faces.
Animaguses are rare and all are supposed to be registered with the Ministry of Magic. One particularly famous animagus, according to author TH White, was the magician Merlin.
Lucifer was an Animagus, not by God’s hand, but perhaps by evolution or by willing it later and he used it in a successful attempt to lead Adam and Eve astray in the Garden of Eden.

senses: Suitable to listen to when driving leisurely.
Suitable for finding sexual partners (especially for gay men).
Tending to cruise for sexual partners.
A laid back job, person, or place.
ety: From cruise + -y.
examples: Will Rogers State Beach is a cruisy gay beach, always lots of people and lots of fun.
Most of the women who approached me were cruisy, butch numbers.

senses: A somewhat granola- or cookie-like chocolate-covered sweet, served in bar form.
An infantry soldier, a grunt.
ety: From crunchy. Use to refer to infantrymen in Vietnam is from their "crunching" through the jungle brush. Use to refer to white Afrikaners is perhaps from their supposed tendency to eat crunchy food.
examples: A different method and a different flavour from the usual brown crunchie. The recipe is easily doubled for a larger batch.

senses: Related to or having the character of dialogue
ety: From dialog + -ical.
examples: Our school favors a dialogical approach to learning.

senses: The bunya pine, Araucaria bidwillii, native to Queensland.
ety: From Yagara bunya bunya, Gabi bunyi, Wakawaka bunyi.
examples: The palm takes the place of the eucalyptus to a certain extent, and the woods teem with the bunya-bunya, — a very desirable and ornamental tree, which belongs to the pine family.

Her three favourite bunyah-bunyah nut trees were destroyed last year to make way for more grazing land for sheep and other animals whose cloven hooves destroyed the delicate topsoil and laid bare the earth.
Bunya nuts, which come from a conifer in the genus Araucaria, are an example of a plant that fruited so heavily that large stores were set aside.

senses: A region or province in Slavic or Slavic-influenced countries.
ety: From a Slavic language, probably Russian о́бласть (óblastʹ, “region, province”), borrowed from Old Church Slavonic область (oblastĭ), from Proto-Slavic *obolstь, from earlier *obvolstь, *obvoldtь, a compound of *o(b)- (“over”) + *volstь (“rule, power, authority”), thus originally probably meaning "a region ruled over". Compare Proto-Slavic *obvoldati (“to rule”).
examples: Almaty oblast (distinct from Almaty city) is the most rural of Kazakhstan's oblasts, at just 22.2 percent urban.

senses: The characteristic or practice of being a fanatic.
ety: From fanatic + -ism.
examples: Witch-hunting became a mania, with all the abuses and excesses which invariably develop with fanaticism.

senses: To wound the pride of (someone); to excite to anger; to irritate, to offend.
To excite (someone) to action, especially by causing jealousy, resentment, etc.; also, to stimulate (an emotion or feeling, especially curiosity or interest).
To pride (oneself) on something.
To take pride in.
To excite to action, especially by causing jealousy, resentment, etc.; also, to stimulate an emotion or feeling, especially curiosity or interest.
ety: The verb is borrowed from French piquer (“to prick, sting; to anger, annoy; (reflexive) to get angry; to provoke, stimulate; (reflexive) to boast about”), from Middle French piquer, picquer (“to prick, sting; to anger, annoy; (reflexive) to get angry”), from Old French piquer (“to pierce with the tip of a sword”), from proto-Romance or Vulgar Latin *pīccare (“to sting; to strike”) or *pikkāre, and then either: * Onomatopoeic; or * from Frankish *pikkōn, from Proto-Germanic *pikkōną (“to knock; to peck; to pick; to prick”). If so, pique is a doublet of pick, pitch, and peck. The noun is borrowe
examples: Brisk Confidence still best with woman copes; / Pique her and soothe in turn, soon Passion crowns thy hopes.
His chusing to walk with her, she had learnt to understand. It was done to pique Miss Brereton.
She treated him indulgently, as if he were a child. He thought he did not mind. But deep below the surface it piqued him.

senses: The state of being final; the condition from which no further changes occur.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French finalité. equivalent to final + -ity.
examples: The finality of my father's death suddenly hit me: there would be no more bedtime stories, no more games of catch in the back yard.
By way of contrast there is an air of finality about the closure of the Welsh Highland Railway.

senses: A one-wheeled attachment to the side of a motorcycle to allow for a separate seat for a passenger or cargo space.
A cocktail made with cognac (or brandy), triple sec liqueur, and lemon juice.
ety: From side + car.
examples: Faux 19th-century bartenders in sleeve garters and baroque facial hair ply their trade in pre-Prohibition bars. Women wearing cloche hats order sidecars at speakeasies.

senses: Existing in name only; nominal.
Named or referred to in the title.
ety: Borrowed from Middle French titulaire, from Latin titulāris, from titulus (“title”).
examples: If these magnific titles yet remain / Not merely titular.
Macbeth is a titular character.
That story begins in rural Wyoming in 1963, when drifters Ennis and Jack are hired by a local rancher to herd sheep through grazing ground on the titular Brokeback Mountain.

senses: Useless; unnecessary; of no value or purpose.
ety: Borrowed from Hindi फालतू (phāltū, “useless, unnecessary”).
examples: Stop wasting time on these faltu arguments.

senses: A fish of the wrasse family found in salt water off of eastern North America from Nova Scotia to South Carolina (Tautoga onitis).
ety: Borrowed from Narragansett tautauog, plural of taut.
examples: The fish he found were nothing unusual: cunner and tautog, small fish generally found around pilings or rocky shores, and one weakfish.

senses: Having a tendency to cling.
ety: From cling + -y.
examples: I conceded I might have slightly mollified if it had been Wendy Rieger in that clingy leopard skin blouse she wears on Channel 4.
